recipe.history:
Swiss cheese — specifically aged Emmentaler — is one of the oldest and most storied cheeses in the world, tracing its roots to the Emme Valley of the canton of Bern in Switzerland. The earliest documented production of Emmentaler dates to the fifteenth century, though the techniques used to craft it almost certainly predate those records by generations. Swiss alpine herdsmen developed the cheese as a means of preserving the extraordinary surplus of summer milk produced at high-altitude pastures. The result was a large-format, hard-rind cheese characterized by its pale ivory interior, its elastic, buttery texture, and — most famously — its walnut-sized holes, or "eyes," formed by carbon dioxide released during the secondary fermentation process driven by Propionibacterium freudenreichii bacteria. Authentic Emmentaler AOP is still produced in large wheels weighing up to 130 kilograms, aged a minimum of four months in temperature-controlled cellars, and rubbed regularly with brine to develop its characteristic sweet, nutty, mildly grassy flavor. The cheese became a symbol of Swiss rural identity, inextricably tied to the pastoral landscape of green valleys and snowcapped peaks, and it earned international renown long before the modern grocery era rendered "Swiss cheese" a generic category of rubbery, mild yellow slices.

Emmentaler made its way to the United States through waves of Swiss and German immigration during the nineteenth century, particularly during the surge of European settlement in the Midwest between the 1840s and 1890s. Swiss immigrant cheesemakers established thriving dairy operations in Wisconsin, Ohio, and Indiana, transplanting their alpine traditions to the American heartland. The Americanized version of Swiss cheese — milder, with smaller eyes and a more uniform texture — eventually became a grocery staple, and by the mid-twentieth century it had earned a permanent place in the American deli and short-order kitchen. Its mild nuttiness and exceptional meltability made it a natural partner for the hamburger. Diners and lunch counters across the country began offering the "Swiss burger" as a slightly more sophisticated alternative to American cheese, and it grew into a beloved classic. The pairing of Swiss cheese with savory beef is today so canonical that it anchors the Reuben, the patty melt, and countless steakhouse burgers — a testament to how thoroughly the cheese embedded itself in the American culinary imagination.

I remember the first time I truly understood what good Swiss cheese could do to a burger. I was nineteen, working a summer job at a marina on Lake Champlain, and there was a tiny diner nearby that made what the owner called his "Swiss mountain burger" — a thick beef patty with aged Emmentaler draped over it while the griddle was still hot, covered with a metal dome to trap steam and let the cheese melt into every crevice. He served it on a pretzel roll, the kind with a dark, lacquered crust and a chewy interior that pushed back when you bit into it. I remember holding that burger in both hands, the cheese pooling at the edges, the salt crystals from the pretzel bun glittering under the fluorescent diner lights. That combination — the earthy nuttiness of the Emmentaler, the toasty, alkaline crunch of the pretzel — felt like a revelation to me. I ate two of them that afternoon, and I have been chasing that memory ever since, adjusting and layering and refining until I landed on this version.

Cooking a burger patty to medium rare — an internal temperature of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is not a preference or a stylistic choice. It is the only correct way to cook a hamburger, full stop. At medium rare, the proteins in the beef have firmed just enough to create structural integrity without seizing and squeezing out the intramuscular fat that gives a good patty its richness and juice. The Maillard reaction on the exterior has built a complex, deeply savory crust while the interior remains a rosy, yielding cushion of flavor. Cook beyond 140 degrees and you are not eating a burger — you are eating a disk of compressed protein that requires condiments to be palatable. The well-done burger is a capitulation to fear, not a culinary decision. Medium rare demands quality beef and confidence, and it rewards both in kind. On this burger especially, the molten Emmentaler needs that yielding, juice-forward interior to pull against — when the cheese is silky and the beef is rare-edged pink, the contrast is what makes each bite complete.
ingredients: 3 1/2 cups bread flour, plus more for kneading
Coarse pretzel salt or flaky sea salt, for topping
For the twisted Swiss cheese melt:
8 oz aged Emmentaler cheese, thinly sliced
4 large shallots, thinly sliced into rings
1 tbsp dry white wine or white wine vinegar
Cornichons or sliced dill pickles, to serve
instructions: 1. Make the pretzel buns: Combine the warm water, sugar, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add the flour, salt, and softened butter. Using the dough hook, mix on low 2 minutes, then increase to medium and knead 8 minutes until the dough is smooth, supple, and slightly tacky. Shape into a ball, place in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let rise at room temperature until doubled, about 1 to 1 1/2 hours.

2. Punch down the risen dough and divide into 4 equal portions (roughly 200g each). Shape each portion into a tight round ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover loosely with a damp towel, and let rest 20 minutes.

3. Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Bring the 8 cups of water to a rolling boil in a wide pot. Add the baking soda carefully — the water will foam vigorously. Working one at a time, lower each dough round into the boiling bath seam-side down and poach for 30 seconds per side. Remove with a slotted spoon, drain briefly, and return to the parchment-lined baking sheet.

4. Brush each boiled bun generously with the beaten egg. Score the top of each bun with a sharp knife or lame — three diagonal slashes or a crosshatch to create the "twisted" appearance. Sprinkle liberally with coarse pretzel salt. Bake 18 to 22 minutes until deep mahogany brown. Transfer to a wire rack and cool at least 15 minutes before slicing.

5. Make the honey–whole-grain mustard aioli: Whisk together the mayonnaise, whole-grain mustard, honey, apple cider vinegar, and salt in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified. Taste and adjust seasoning. Cover and refrigerate until needed.

6. Make the caramelized shallots: Melt the butter with the olive oil in a medium skillet over medium-low heat. Add the shallot rings and salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, for 25 to 30 minutes until deeply golden and jammy. Add the thyme leaves and white wine, stir to deglaze, and cook 2 more minutes. Remove from heat and set aside.

7. Form the burger patties: Divide the ground beef into 4 equal portions (8 oz / 227g each). Handle the beef as little as possible. Shape each portion into a patty approximately 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick. Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple into the center of each patty to prevent doming during cooking. Season both sides generously with kosher salt and cracked black pepper immediately before cooking.

8. Heat a cast-iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking. Cook the patties 3 to 4 minutes on the first side without pressing or moving them, until a deep brown crust forms. Flip once. Immediately layer the Emmentaler slices over each patty — 2 to 3 slices per patty, overlapping. Place a metal dome, inverted bowl, or tight-fitting lid over the pan and add 1 tablespoon of water to the pan to generate steam. Cook 2 to 3 minutes more until the internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) on an instant-read thermometer and the cheese is fully melted and beginning to run down the sides. Remove patties to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
9. While the patties rest, split the pretzel buns horizontally and toast the cut sides on the hot skillet or griddle for 1 to 2 minutes until lightly charred.

10. Assemble the burgers: Spread the honey–whole-grain mustard aioli generously on both the top and bottom bun halves. On the bottom bun, layer a leaf of butter lettuce and 2 slices of tomato. Place the melted-cheese-crowned patty on top. Pile the caramelized shallots over the cheese. Cap with the top bun. Serve immediately alongside cornichons.
